overview: Birger Magnusson was Swedish king whose reign collapsed amid conflict with his brothers and noble factions. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1290 — Becomes king; 1317 — Nyköping Banquet; 1318 — Deposed.
He died in 1321, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Birger Magnusson was born c. 1280. His family background is usually placed in House of Bjälbo, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.
Birger Magnusson's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Birger Magnusson of Sweden is remembered for one of the most notorious acts of treachery in Scandinavian history: the Nyköping Banquet of 1317, at which he seized and imprisoned his own brothers, the dukes Erik and Valdemar, and left them to die in captivity, reportedly of starvation. That single act of fratricidal revenge dominates his reputation.

The deed grew out of years of bitter conflict among the royal brothers, and Birger's vengeance backfired catastrophically: the outrage provoked a rebellion that drove him from the throne and into exile, and led to the execution of his son. The sources present him as vindictive and politically disastrous, undone by the very cruelty meant to secure him.

Little of his character survives apart from this dark episode, but it is enough to fix his memory firmly. He is remembered as the king whose act of treacherous revenge destroyed his own rule — a figure of dynastic tragedy whose name is bound permanently to the Nyköping Banquet.

contentSections.title: As king of Sweden
paragraphs: Birger became king as a child after Magnus III. His reign was dominated by conflict with his brothers Erik and Valdemar, culminating in imprisonment, revenge, and civil war.
As King of Sweden, Birger Magnusson had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in exile in Denmark after deposition, following the political disaster of the Nyköping Banquet and civil conflict.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His reign is remembered as a crisis of Bjälbo kingship and a prelude to Magnus Eriksson’s accession.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Birger Magnusson's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Birger Magnusson was born around c. 1280, but the birthplace is not securely recorded. The date is approximate, but it places the early life in the setting of Kingdom of Sweden.

timeline.title: Becomes king
timeline.description: Birger became king after Magnus III, but his reign was overshadowed by rivalry with his brothers Erik and Valdemar.

timeline.title: Nyköping Banquet
timeline.description: At the Nyköping Banquet, Birger imprisoned his brothers; their deaths triggered outrage and destroyed his political position.

timeline.title: Deposed
timeline.description: Birger was driven from power after the backlash to Nyköping, ending his rule and forcing him into exile.
